questions.question: Explain how to set up the thermistor potential divider circuit so the air conditioning switches on when the room is hot, using particle behaviour of an NTC thermistor.
questions.answer: Connect the secondary (air-conditioning) circuit across the fixed resistor XY. When the room is hot the thermistor resistance falls, so the p.d. across XY rises above the switch-on value.
steps: Choice of connection: in the series circuit the p.d. divides in proportion to resistance. The aircon must switch on when it is hot, so the secondary circuit is connected across the fixed resistor XY (not across the thermistor YZ).

Particle explanation of an NTC thermistor: as the temperature rises, more electrons gain enough energy to leave their atoms and become conduction electrons, so the number of charge carriers per unit volume increases.
This outweighs the larger lattice vibrations, so the thermistor resistance decreases as the room gets hotter.
The total resistance of the series circuit falls, so the current rises (I = E / R_total).
The p.d. across the fixed resistor is V = I R (R constant), so it rises, while the p.d. across the thermistor YZ falls.
When the p.d. across XY exceeds the set value, the secondary circuit switches the air-conditioning on, which cools the room; as it cools the p.d. falls and the unit switches off.

questions.question: Fixed resistor 1.20 k ohm in series with LDR across 12.0 V (negligible internal resistance). Voltmeter across LDR reads 4.71 V in dark and 2.16 V in light. Find the change in LDR resistance.
questions.answer: Change in resistance = -512 ohm (about 510 ohm decrease)
steps: Fixed resistor and LDR are in series, so their p.d.s add to 12.0 V.
Dark: p.d. across fixed resistor = 12.0 - 4.71 = 7.29 V.
Current (same through both) I = 7.29 / 1200 = 6.08 x 10^-3 A.
Dark LDR resistance = 4.71 / 6.08 x 10^-3 = 775 ohm.
Light: p.d. across fixed resistor = 12.0 - 2.16 = 9.84 V; I = 9.84 / 1200 = 8.20 x 10^-3 A.
Light LDR resistance = 2.16 / 8.20 x 10^-3 = 263 ohm.
Change = 263 - 775 = -512 ohm, so the resistance falls by about 510 ohm.

questions.question: Complete a circuit diagram to determine the e.m.f. and internal resistance of a potato cell.
questions.answer: Add an ammeter and a variable resistor in series with the potato cell, and a voltmeter connected in parallel across the cell.
steps: In the gap of the main wire draw an ammeter in series with the cell, to measure the current I.
Also in series draw a variable resistor (rheostat), so that I can be varied to take several readings.
Connect a voltmeter in parallel with the potato cell (directly across its two electrodes) to measure the terminal p.d. V.
Then V = E - I r, so a graph of V against I gives E and r.

questions.question: From a graph of p.d. V against current I for a potato cell, determine its e.m.f. and internal resistance.
questions.answer: E.m.f. = 0.29 V; internal resistance = 4.3 x 10^2 ohm
steps: Terminal p.d. V = e.m.f. - I r, so the graph of V against I is a straight line with intercept e.m.f. and gradient -r.
Draw a best-fit line through the points. It meets the V axis at about 0.29 V, so the e.m.f. is about 0.29 V.
Take two well-separated points on the line, e.g. (0.10 mA, 0.244 V) and (0.40 mA, 0.116 V): gradient = (0.116 - 0.244) / (0.40 - 0.10) = -0.43 V per mA.
Current is in mA, so |gradient| = 0.43 V / 10^-3 A = 4.3 x 10^2 ohm, which is the internal resistance r.

questions.question: Two resistors each of resistance R are connected to a battery of e.m.f. E and internal resistance r, first in series (A) then in parallel (B). Which arrangement gives the greater terminal p.d.?
questions.answer: Series arrangement A gives the greater terminal p.d.
steps: Terminal p.d. V = E x R_ext / (R_ext + r), where R_ext is the external resistance.
Series: R_ext = 2R, so V_A = 2RE / (2R + r).
Parallel: R_ext = R/2, so V_B = (R/2)E / (R/2 + r) = RE / (R + 2r).
Ratio V_A / V_B = 2(R + 2r) / (2R + r) = (2R + 4r) / (2R + r), which is greater than 1 because 4r > r.
So V_A > V_B: the series arrangement gives the greater terminal p.d. (more external resistance means less lost to internal resistance).

questions.question: Wires P and Q are in series. P has carrier density n and diameter d, drift velocity v. Q has carrier density 2n and diameter 2d. Find the drift velocity in Q.
questions.answer: A: v/8
steps: The wires are in series, so the current I is the same in both.
Using I = n A v e: Q has n_Q = 2n and A_Q = 4 A_P (diameter 2d gives 4 times the area).
n A v = (2n)(4A) v_Q, so v_Q = v / 8.

questions.question: Which of the following is an SI unit for e.m.f.? A coulomb, B joule, C newton, D volt.
questions.answer: D (volt)
steps: EMF is energy transferred per unit charge: E = W/Q.
Units: joule per coulomb (J C^-1).
1 volt = 1 J C^-1, so the answer is D.

questions.question: Cell of e.m.f. E and internal resistance r supplies current I with terminal p.d. V. Which expression gives the power dissipated in the internal resistance? A P = I(E - V), B P = I^2 R, C P = I..., D P = V^2/r.
questions.answer: A, P = I(E - V)
steps: Power in internal resistance P = I^2 r.
Lost p.d. inside the cell is Ir = E - V (E is split between external and internal parts).
So P = I x Ir = I(E - V), which is option A.
Option B uses R (external resistance), so it is not the internal power.

questions.question: Which graph shows how power P dissipated by an ohmic conductor varies with p.d. V across it?
questions.answer: D
steps: For an ohmic conductor R is constant and P = V^2 / R, so P is proportional to V^2.
The graph of P against V is therefore a curve through the origin whose gradient increases with V (a parabola), which is graph D.
A is constant P, B is a straight line (P proportional to V), C is flattening, so none of these match.

questions.question: Derive an equation for the combined resistance RT of two resistors R1 and R2 in series.
questions.answer: RT = R1 + R2
steps: In series the same current I flows through both resistors.
Total p.d. is the sum of the p.d.s: V = V1 + V2.
Using V = IR: I RT = I R1 + I R2.
Divide by I: RT = R1 + R2.

questions.question: A resistor combination with an ammeter reading 0.50 A (negligible internal battery resistance) is shown. Calculate resistance R.
questions.answer: R = 12 ohm
steps: Total resistance from the battery: R_total = V / I = 7.0 V / 0.50 A = 14 ohm.
The 6.0 ohm resistor is in series with the parallel section, so the parallel section has 14 - 6.0 = 8.0 ohm.
The 8.0 ohm and 16.0 ohm resistors are in series: 24.0 ohm. R is in parallel with this: 1/8.0 = 1/R + 1/24.0.

questions.question: In daylight an LDR has resistance 670 ohm; the fixed resistor is 8.00 k ohm. Calculate the power in the fixed resistor.
steps: The LDR and the fixed resistor are in series across the 12.0 V battery (negligible internal resistance).
Power in the fixed resistor P = I^2 R = (1.38 x 10^-3)^2 x 8000 = 1.5 x 10^-2 W (0.015 W).

questions.question: Explain why the power in the fixed resistor decreases as light intensity on an LDR decreases, referring to electrons in the LDR.
questions.answer: Lower light gives fewer electrons promoted to the conduction band, so the LDR resistance rises, the current falls and P = I^2 R in the fixed resistor decreases.
steps: Lower light intensity means fewer photons, so fewer electrons are excited into the conduction band.
Fewer charge carriers (free electrons) means the LDR resistance increases.
Total resistance in the series circuit increases, so the current I = E / R_total decreases.
Power in the fixed resistor P = I^2 R decreases because I has decreased (R is constant).

questions.question: Potential divider with battery (negligible internal resistance) and LDR; voltmeter across fixed resistor. Which statement is correct? A LDR resistance halves so reading halves; B increasing light decreases reading; C increasing light has no effect; D reading plus LDR p.d. always equals 12.0 V.
questions.answer: D
steps: Fixed resistor and LDR are in series across the battery, so their p.d.s always sum to the e.m.f. (12.0 V).
A is wrong: the p.d. does not simply halve when R halves (it depends on the ratio of resistances).
B is wrong: more light lowers LDR resistance, so the p.d. across the fixed resistor increases.
C is wrong: light intensity changes the reading.
D is correct by the series voltage rule.

questions.question: A negative temperature coefficient thermistor is in a circuit with meters V1, V2 and A. The thermistor temperature increases. Which table row shows the meter readings?
questions.answer: A: V1 decreases, V2 increases, A increases
steps: As the temperature of an NTC thermistor rises, more conduction electrons are released and its resistance falls.
The total resistance falls, so the current (ammeter A) increases.
V2 is across the fixed resistor, so V2 = I R increases; V1 (across the thermistor) = E - V2 decreases. This is row A.

questions.question: Calculate the voltmeter reading for the circuit shown.
questions.answer: Voltmeter reading = 1.2 V
steps: The 12 k ohm and 55 k ohm resistors are in series with the 1.5 V cell, and the voltmeter is across the 55 k ohm resistor.
Potential divider: V = 1.5 x 55 / (12 + 55) = 1.5 x 0.821.

questions.question: A student measures a voltmeter reading lower than calculated in (a). Explain two reasons.
questions.answer: (1) The cell has internal resistance, so its terminal p.d. is less than 1.5 V. (2) The voltmeter has a finite resistance, which lowers the resistance of the parallel combination across the 55 k ohm resistor.
steps: Reason 1: the cell has internal resistance r, so there are lost volts I r. The p.d. available to the two resistors is below 1.5 V, so the voltmeter reads less than the calculated value.
Reason 2: the voltmeter does not have infinite resistance. It draws current, so the effective resistance of the 55 k ohm resistor and voltmeter in parallel is less than 55 k ohm.
A smaller resistance in this section takes a smaller share of the cell p.d. (potential divider), so the reading is lower.

questions.question: Two 5 ohm resistors are in series and in parallel. Which table row shows the total resistances?
questions.answer: D: series 10 ohm, parallel 2.5 ohm
steps: Series: R_T = 5 + 5 = 10 ohm.
Parallel: 1/R_T = 1/5 + 1/5 = 2/5, so R_T = 2.5 ohm. This is row D.

questions.question: State what is meant by e.m.f.
questions.answer: E.m.f. is the energy transferred per unit charge by the source (from chemical to electrical energy) in driving charge round the whole circuit.
steps: E.m.f. is the energy transferred per unit charge passing through the source.
Equivalently, it is the total energy per coulomb supplied by the cell, including energy lost inside it.

questions.question: Car battery emf 12.00 V. Voltmeter reads 11.81 V and ammeter reads 9.83 A. Calculate the internal resistance.
questions.answer: r = 0.019 ohm (about 0.0193 ohm)
steps: Lost p.d. inside the battery = E - V = 12.00 - 11.81 = 0.19 V.
Ohm's law for internal resistance: r = (E - V) / I = 0.19 / 9.83.
r = 0.0193 ohm, about 0.019 ohm.

questions.question: Describe how readings of ammeter and voltmeter from several resistor settings can be used graphically to find internal resistance.
questions.answer: Plot V (y) against I (x); the gradient magnitude gives r and the y-intercept gives E.
steps: Adjust the variable resistor and record V and I for several settings.
Plot a graph of terminal p.d. V against current I (V on the y-axis).
The equation V = E - Ir is a straight line with gradient -r.
Find the gradient of the best-fit line and take its magnitude: this is the internal resistance r.
The y-intercept (current = 0) gives the e.m.f. E.

questions.question: A 9.0 V cell with internal resistance 0.10 ohm supplies a 5.0 ohm resistor. The student claims that when r rises to 0.50 ohm, the power in the resistor falls to 70% of original. Is this correct?
questions.answer: Not correct: the power falls to about 86% of the original value.
steps: Ratio = 13.4 / 15.6 = 0.86, so the power is about 86% of its original value.
86% is not 70%, so the student's conclusion is incorrect.

questions.question: A lightning strike 1 km away gives a 3 s delay before thunder. Speed of sound is 340 m/s. Determine whether the teacher is correct.
questions.answer: Approximately correct: the delay is about 2.9 s, which rounds to 3 s.
steps: Time t = distance / speed = 1000 / 340.
t = 2.94 s, which is about 3 s to one significant figure.
The teacher is essentially correct; the light arrives almost instantly so the delay is due only to the sound.

questions.question: Current 25 000 A flows for 30 s in a lightning strike. Calculate the total charge transferred.
steps: Charge Q = I t (charge is current multiplied by time).

questions.question: Potential difference 1.2 x 10^9 V and current 25 000 A. Calculate the power dissipated by the lightning strike.
steps: Power P = V x I (p.d. multiplied by current).

questions.question: Show that the resistivity of air in the lightning channel is about 0.2 ohm m, using distance 400 m, current 25 000 A, p.d. 1.2 x 10^9 V and diameter 5.0 cm.
questions.answer: Resistivity = 0.24 ohm m, which is about 0.2 ohm m.
steps: Resistance R = V / I = 1.2 x 10^9 / 2.5 x 10^4 = 4.8 x 10^4 ohm.
Cross-sectional area A = pi r^2 with r = 0.025 m: A = 1.96 x 10^-3 m^2.
Resistivity rho = R A / L = (4.8 x 10^4 x 1.96 x 10^-3) / 400.
rho = 94.2 / 400 = 0.24 ohm m, about 0.2 ohm m as required.

questions.question: The accepted resistivity of air is 10^16 ohm m. Suggest why the value calculated from the data is much smaller.
questions.answer: The lightning heats and ionises the air in the channel, creating many free charge carriers, so it conducts far better than normal air.
steps: Normal air is an almost perfect insulator, so its resistivity is very high.
The strike ionises the air in the channel, producing many free electrons and ions.
More charge carriers means much lower resistivity, so the calculated value is far smaller.

questions.question: Explain the process by which nitrogen atoms produce a line spectrum.
questions.answer: Electrons are excited to higher energy levels by collisions and then fall back, emitting photons of discrete frequencies.
steps: Energy from the lightning strike (collisions) excites electrons in nitrogen atoms to higher energy levels.
Electrons then fall back to lower energy levels (de-excitation).
Each fall releases a photon with energy equal to the energy difference, E = hf.
Because the energy levels are discrete, only certain frequencies are emitted, giving a line spectrum.

questions.question: State why the line spectrum from oxygen atoms would differ from that of nitrogen atoms.
questions.answer: Oxygen and nitrogen atoms have different energy level structures, so their emitted photon energies (frequencies) differ.
steps: Each element has its own set of electron energy levels.
So the energy differences between levels, and hence photon frequencies, differ for each element.

questions.question: Which statement about physical quantities or units is correct? A current is derived; B power is derived; C coulomb is a base unit; D volt is a base unit.
questions.answer: B
steps: Current is a SI base quantity (ampere is a base unit), so A is wrong.
Power is derived (energy divided by time), so B is correct.
The coulomb is derived (A s), so C is wrong.
The volt is derived (J C^-1), so D is wrong.

questions.question: Four identical 2.0 ohm resistors A, B, C and D in a circuit. Determine the power dissipated in each resistor.
steps: B and C are in series: 4.0 ohm. In parallel with D (2.0 ohm): R = 4.0 x 2.0 / 6.0 = 1.33 ohm. Total R = 2.0 + 1.33 = 3.33 ohm.
Current from the 10 V battery (taking its internal resistance as negligible): I = 10 / 3.33 = 3.0 A. Power in A: P = I^2 R = 3.0^2 x 2.0 = 18 W.
P.d. across the parallel section = 3.0 x 1.33 = 4.0 V. Power in D: V^2 / R = 4.0^2 / 2.0 = 8.0 W.
Current in B and C = 4.0 / 4.0 = 1.0 A, so P = I^2 R = 1.0^2 x 2.0 = 2.0 W for each of B and C.

questions.question: Explain, without calculation, what happens to the power in resistor A if resistor D is disconnected.
questions.answer: The power dissipated in A decreases.
steps: Disconnecting D removes a parallel branch, so the resistance of the section containing B and C rises (from 1.33 ohm to 4.0 ohm).
The total resistance of the circuit increases, so with a fixed e.m.f. the current falls.
Resistor A carries the total current and P = I^2 R with R fixed, so the power in A decreases (to about 5.6 W).

questions.question: Explain, in terms of particles, why the resistance of a filament lamp increases as the p.d. across it increases.
questions.answer: Higher p.d. gives higher current and more energy in the filament, so the metal ions vibrate more and collisions with electrons increase, raising resistance.
steps: Greater p.d. drives more current through the filament.
Greater current means more energy is transferred to the filament, so it heats up.
The metal ions in the lattice vibrate with greater amplitude.
Electrons collide more frequently with the vibrating ions, reducing their drift velocity for a given field, so resistance increases.

questions.question: With a voltmeter reading of 3.42 V in a thermistor circuit, determine the temperature of the thermistor.
questions.answer: About 34 degrees C
steps: The voltmeter is across the 11.5 ohm resistor, so I = 3.42 / 11.5 = 0.297 A.
P.d. across the thermistor = 9.00 - 3.42 = 5.58 V.
R_thermistor = V / I = 5.58 / 0.297 = 18.8 ohm.
On the graph, a resistance of 18.8 ohm corresponds to a temperature of about 34 degrees C.

questions.question: Assess whether doubling the e.m.f. of the battery will double the voltmeter reading.
questions.answer: Correct: with negligible internal resistance, every p.d. in the circuit is proportional to the e.m.f., so doubling it doubles the voltmeter reading (provided the thermistor resistance is unchanged).
steps: The battery has negligible internal resistance, so the full e.m.f. appears across the external circuit.
The current I = E / R_total is proportional to E for a fixed total resistance.
Each p.d. V = IR is therefore proportional to E.
Doubling E doubles the current and the voltmeter reading, so the student is correct, as long as the thermistor temperature (and resistance) does not change.

questions.question: Derive a formula for the total resistance RT of two resistors R1 and R2 in parallel.
steps: In parallel each resistor has the same p.d. V across it.
Total current I = I1 + I2.
Using I = V/R: V/RT = V/R1 + V/R2.
Divide by V: 1/RT = 1/R1 + 1/R2.

questions.question: Five 5.0 ohm resistors M, N, O, P, Q form a combination. Show that the resistance between A and B is about 3 ohm.
questions.answer: R_AB = 3.1 ohm (about 3 ohm)
steps: P and Q are in series: 5.0 + 5.0 = 10 ohm. This is in parallel with N (5.0 ohm): 1/R = 1/5.0 + 1/10 = 3/10, so R = 3.33 ohm.
This combination is in series with O: 3.33 + 5.0 = 8.33 ohm.
That branch is in parallel with M (5.0 ohm): 1/R = 1/5.0 + 1/8.33 = 0.32, so R_AB = 3.1 ohm, which is about 3 ohm.

questions.question: Explain which 5.0 ohm resistor should be replaced with a 20.0 ohm resistor to make the resistance between A and B greater than 5.0 ohm, without the arrangement changing.
questions.answer: Replace resistor M.
steps: M is connected directly between A and B, in parallel with all the other resistors.
The combined resistance of a parallel arrangement is always smaller than the smallest branch resistance. With M = 5.0 ohm unchanged, the total can never be more than 5.0 ohm.
Replacing M with 20.0 ohm removes this limit; the resistance becomes 20 x 8.33 / (20 + 8.33) = 5.9 ohm, which is greater than 5.0 ohm.

questions.question: Circuit with variable resistor R used to find internal resistance r and e.m.f. of a cell. Which expression gives the current in the cell?
questions.answer: C: E / (R + r)
steps: The cell (internal resistance r) is in series with the variable resistor R, so the total resistance is R + r.
The current is I = E / (R + r), which is option C.

questions.question: A combination of three resistors X, Y, Z is shown. Which expression gives the total resistance?
questions.answer: C: X + YZ / (Y + Z)
steps: Y and Z are in parallel: 1/R = 1/Y + 1/Z, so R = YZ / (Y + Z).
X is in series with this section, so R_T = X + YZ / (Y + Z), option C.

questions.question: Circuit used for emf and internal resistance of a cell; V (y-axis) against I (x-axis) graph. Which statement is correct? A area under graph is energy dissipated in cell; B gradient is r; C V and I are directly proportional; D y-intercept is the e.m.f.
questions.answer: D
steps: V = E - Ir is a straight line with a negative gradient, so it is not directly proportional (C is wrong).
The gradient is -r, so B is wrong (magnitude r, sign negative).
The y-intercept (I = 0) gives the e.m.f. E, so D is correct.
The area under the V-I graph is power (V x I), not energy, so A is wrong.

questions.question: Current carrying wire AB of length x and uniform diameter; slider S moved until voltmeter reads 0 V. Which equation is correct?
questions.answer: B: y / (x - y) = R1 / R2
steps: The wire AB and the chain R1, R2 are two potential dividers across the same battery.
The voltmeter reads 0 when the slider S is at the same potential as the junction of R1 and R2, so the p.d. across length y of the wire equals the p.d. across R1.
For a uniform wire: y / x = R1 / (R1 + R2).
Rearranging: y (R1 + R2) = x R1, so y R2 = (x - y) R1, which gives y / (x - y) = R1 / R2, option B.

questions.question: Wire of diameter 0.181 mm, length 55.0 cm, resistivity 1.10 x 10^-6 ohm m. Show that one resistor has resistance about 24 ohm.
questions.answer: R = 23.5 ohm, about 24 ohm.
steps: Cross-sectional area A = pi d^2 / 4 = pi (0.181 x 10^-3)^2 / 4 = 2.57 x 10^-8 m^2.
R = 6.05 x 10^-7 / 2.57 x 10^-8 = 23.5 ohm, about 24 ohm as required.

questions.question: A student suggests the maximum power output from the resistors in the circuit is greater than 12 W. Assess this suggestion.
questions.answer: The suggestion is not correct: the maximum power is about 9.2 W, which is less than 12 W.
steps: Maximum power needs the smallest resistance, which is with both switches closed.
The branch with X has two resistors (47.0 ohm) in parallel with the branch with Y (23.5 ohm): R = 47.0 x 23.5 / 70.5 = 15.7 ohm.
This is less than 12 W (and the wire resistance rises when it warms up, which would lower the power further), so the student is wrong.

questions.question: With switch X open and switch Y closed, calculate the number of conduction electrons passing through the resistor each second immediately after Y is closed.
questions.answer: Number of electrons per second = 3.2 x 10^18
steps: With X open and Y closed, only one resistor (23.5 ohm) is connected to the 12.0 V battery.
Number of electrons per second = I / e = 0.51 / 1.60 x 10^-19 = 3.2 x 10^18 s^-1.

questions.question: After switch Y has been closed for a few minutes the power dissipated by the resistor decreases. Explain why.
questions.answer: The wire heats up, so its resistance increases and the current (and power) decreases.
steps: The current heats the resistor wire, so the temperature of the metal rises.
The lattice ions vibrate with greater amplitude, so the conduction electrons collide with them more often, and the resistance of the wire increases.
The p.d. stays at 12.0 V, so I falls and P = V^2 / R decreases.

questions.question: Lamp marked 12 V 60 W, filament diameter 0.25 mm, resistivity 5.6 x 10^-8 ohm m at operating temperature. Calculate the length of the filament wire.
steps: Resistance at normal operation R = V^2 / P = 12^2 / 60 = 2.40 ohm.
Cross-sectional area A = pi (d/2)^2 = pi (0.125 x 10^-3)^2 = 4.91 x 10^-8 m^2.

questions.question: Lamps A (12 V 60 W) and B (12 V 30 W) are in a circuit; a student says both operate normally. Evaluate this.
questions.answer: The statement is not correct: A gets about 8 V (dimmer than normal) and B gets about 16 V (above its 12 V rating).
steps: Lamp A: R = V^2 / P = 12^2 / 60 = 2.4 ohm (rated current 5.0 A). Lamp B: R = 12^2 / 30 = 4.8 ohm (rated current 2.5 A).
In series across 24 V (assuming these resistances), R_total = 7.2 ohm, so I = 24 / 7.2 = 3.3 A.
P.d. across A = 3.3 x 2.4 = 8.0 V (less than 12 V, so A is dim), and across B = 3.3 x 4.8 = 16 V (more than 12 V, so B is overloaded).
The lamps do not both work normally. Normal operation would need 5.0 A through A and 2.5 A through B, which cannot happen in series.

questions.question: Cell e.m.f. 1.50 V, voltmeter reads 1.19 V with lights off. Calculate the LDR resistance in the dark.
questions.answer: Resistance of LDR = 1.3 x 10^3 ohm
steps: The voltmeter is across the 5.00 k ohm resistor, so I = 1.19 / 5000 = 2.38 x 10^-4 A.
P.d. across the LDR = 1.50 - 1.19 = 0.31 V.

questions.question: With lights on the LDR is about 9 ohm. Explain why the circuit cannot determine the LDR resistance with the lights on, given the voltmeter resolution of 0.01 V.
questions.answer: With R_LDR of 9 ohm, the p.d. across the LDR is only about 0.003 V, less than the 0.01 V resolution, so the voltmeter reads 1.50 V.
steps: With the lights on, R_LDR is about 9 ohm compared with 5000 ohm, so the p.d. across the fixed resistor is 1.50 x 5000 / 5009 = 1.497 V.
The voltmeter has a resolution of 0.01 V, so it displays 1.50 V, the same as the e.m.f.
The p.d. across the LDR (1.50 - 1.50 = 0 V, really about 0.003 V) is smaller than the resolution, so it cannot be measured and the resistance cannot be calculated.

questions.question: Complete the circuit diagram for a nichrome resistivity experiment with ammeter, voltmeter and variable resistor.
questions.answer: Connect a cell, the ammeter and the variable resistor in series with the nichrome wire, and connect the voltmeter in parallel across the nichrome wire.
steps: Join the two ends of the wire to a series loop containing a cell (or power supply), a variable resistor and an ammeter.
The variable resistor lets the current be kept at 0.200 A as the wire length changes.
Connect the voltmeter in parallel across the nichrome wire only (between the two dots), so it reads the p.d. across the wire.

questions.question: From a graph of p.d. against length (current 0.200 A, area 5.31 x 10^-8 m^2), determine the resistivity of nichrome.
questions.answer: Resistivity = 1.1 x 10^-6 ohm m
steps: R = V / I and R = rho L / A, so V = (I rho / A) L. The gradient of the V against L graph is I rho / A.
Gradient = (4.13 - 0) V / (1.00 - 0) m = 4.13 V m^-1 (read from the best-fit line).
rho = gradient x A / I = 4.13 x 5.31 x 10^-8 / 0.200.
rho = 1.1 x 10^-6 ohm m.

questions.question: Calculate the power dissipated from nichrome wire of length 0.75 m with current 0.200 A.
questions.answer: Power = 0.62 W
steps: From the line, a length of 0.75 m has p.d. V = 4.13 V m^-1 x 0.75 m = 3.10 V.
The current is 0.200 A, so P = V I = 3.10 x 0.200.

questions.question: Cell in series with variable resistor R = 12 ohm; ammeter reads 107 mA; 50 J transferred by the cell in 300 s. Calculate the internal resistance r.
questions.answer: r = 2.6 ohm
steps: Energy transferred by cell E_total = E x I x t, so E = 50 / (0.107 x 300) = 1.56 V.
Circuit equation: E = I (R + r), so R + r = 1.56 / 0.107 = 14.6 ohm.

questions.question: Increasing R makes the terminal p.d. closer to the e.m.f. Explain why, without calculation.
questions.answer: Increasing R reduces the current, so the lost volts Ir inside the cell fall and the terminal p.d. rises towards the e.m.f.
steps: Increasing R increases total resistance, so current I = E/(R + r) decreases.
The lost volts Ir inside the cell decrease.
Terminal p.d. V = E - Ir therefore increases towards E.

questions.question: A voltmeter is added to the circuit. Explain how this circuit can determine r using a graph.
questions.answer: Plot V (voltmeter across R) against I; the y-intercept is the e.m.f. and the gradient is -r.
steps: The voltmeter across the variable resistor reads the terminal p.d., V = E - I r.
Vary R, and record the voltmeter reading V and the ammeter reading I (convert mA to A) for several values.
Plot V on the y-axis against I on the x-axis; this gives a straight line with a negative gradient.
Compare with y = c + m x: the gradient equals -r, so r = -gradient (and the intercept on the V axis gives the e.m.f.).

questions.question: Explain why the voltmeter reads less than 9.0 V when the switch is closed.
questions.answer: With the switch closed a current flows, so p.d. is lost across the battery's internal resistance, and the terminal p.d. is less than the e.m.f.
steps: Closing the switch creates a current in the circuit.
The battery's internal resistance has a current through it, so p.d. Ir is lost inside the battery.
Terminal p.d. = E - Ir, which is less than the e.m.f. of 9.0 V.

questions.question: Battery emf 9.0 V, internal resistance 15 ohm, resistor 270 ohm. Calculate the voltmeter reading when the switch is closed.
steps: Total resistance = 270 + 15 = 285 ohm, so I = 9.0 / 285 = 0.0316 A.
Terminal p.d. = I x 270 = 0.0316 x 270 = 8.5 V.
Alternatively V = E R / (R + r) = 9.0 x 270 / 285 = 8.5 V.

questions.question: With the switch closed 12 C of charge flows through the battery. Calculate the decrease in chemical energy store.
steps: Energy transferred from chemical store = charge x e.m.f. (energy per coulomb).
E = Q x EMF = 12 C x 9.0 V = 108 J.

questions.question: Determine the milliammeter reading when the thermistor temperature is 54 C.
questions.answer: Milliammeter reading = 9.0 mA
steps: From the graph, the thermistor resistance at 54 degrees C is about 1.0 k ohm.
The 3.0 k ohm resistor and thermistor are in series: 4.0 k ohm. This branch and the 2.0 k ohm resistor are both across the 12 V battery.
Current in the 2.0 k ohm branch = 12 / 2000 = 6.0 mA. Current in the other branch = 12 / 4000 = 3.0 mA.
The milliammeter is in the main line and reads the total current: 6.0 + 3.0 = 9.0 mA.

questions.question: Explain how decreasing the thermistor temperature affects the voltmeter reading, without calculation.
questions.answer: The voltmeter reading increases.
steps: Decreasing the temperature of the NTC thermistor means fewer conduction electrons are released, so its resistance increases.
The thermistor and the 3.0 k ohm resistor form a potential divider across the 12 V battery (negligible internal resistance).
The thermistor now has a larger share of the total resistance of this branch, so it takes a larger share of the 12 V and the voltmeter reading increases.

questions.topic: Power in Fixed Resistor at Lower Temperature
questions.question: Explain how decreasing the thermistor temperature affects the power dissipated by the 2.0 k ohm resistor, without calculation.
questions.answer: The power in the 2.0 k ohm resistor stays the same.
steps: The 2.0 k ohm resistor is connected directly across the battery, in parallel with the other branch.
The battery has negligible internal resistance, so the p.d. across it stays at 12 V whatever the thermistor does.
With V and R both unchanged, P = V^2 / R is unchanged.

questions.question: Draw a circuit diagram to determine the e.m.f. and internal resistance of a cell using an ammeter and voltmeter.
questions.answer: Cell in series with an ammeter and a variable resistor; voltmeter connected in parallel across the cell terminals.
steps: Draw a series loop: the cell, an ammeter and a variable resistor (rheostat).
Connect a voltmeter across the cell terminals (in parallel with the cell, and not across the ammeter) so that it reads the terminal p.d.
Label the symbols correctly (cell, ammeter A in a circle, voltmeter V in a circle, variable resistor with an arrow).

questions.topic: EMF and Internal Resistance from V-I Graph
questions.question: Explain how the e.m.f. and internal resistance can be determined from a graph of terminal p.d. against current.
questions.answer: The y-intercept is the e.m.f.; the magnitude of the gradient is the internal resistance r.
steps: The terminal p.d. is V = E - I r, which compares with y = c + m x.
The intercept on the V axis (where I = 0) equals the e.m.f. E.
The gradient of the straight line is -r, so r = -(change in V / change in I), found with a large triangle on the line.

questions.question: Cell of e.m.f. E and internal resistance r is in series with resistors R1 and R2 carrying current I; V1 is the p.d. across R1. Which expression is correct? A E = V1 + Ir; B E = IR1 + Ir; C E = IR2 + Ir; D E = V1 + IR2 + Ir.
questions.answer: D
steps: Energy conservation round the series circuit: E = (p.d. across R1) + (p.d. across R2) + (lost volts in r).
p.d. across R1 = V1, across R2 = IR2, lost volts = Ir.
So E = V1 + IR2 + Ir, which is option D.
Option A omits R2, B and C each omit one of the resistor p.d.s.

questions.question: A battery is connected to identical uniform nichrome wires PQ and RS, with a voltmeter connected as shown. Which is the voltmeter reading? A 1.0 V, B 2.0 V, C 3.0 V, D 4.0 V.
steps: Both identical wires are across the 4.0 V battery, so each has a p.d. that falls uniformly along its length at 4.0 V m^-1 (each wire is 1.00 m long).
The voltmeter is connected 0.25 m along PQ and 0.75 m along RS, and P and R are at the same potential.
So the potentials differ by (0.75 - 0.25) m x 4.0 V m^-1 = 2.0 V.

questions.question: LDR and fixed resistor in circuit; light intensity on LDR increases. Which does not take place? A current increases; B p.d. across fixed resistor increases; C total power decreases; D LDR resistance decreases.
questions.answer: C
steps: Light intensity up means LDR resistance falls (D occurs).
Total resistance falls, so current increases (A occurs), and p.d. across the fixed resistor increases (B occurs).
Total power = E x I, and E is constant while I increases, so total power increases. C does not take place.

questions.question: Show that the power of the LED is about 0.1 W, given the ammeter reads 9.2 mA.
steps: The LED is connected directly across the 12.0 V battery (negligible internal resistance), so its p.d. is 12.0 V.
The ammeter reads the current through the LED: I = 9.2 mA = 9.2 x 10^-3 A.
P = V I = 12.0 x 9.2 x 10^-3 = 0.11 W, which is about 0.1 W.

questions.question: LED of wavelength 627 nm, 100% efficient, power about 0.1 W. Calculate the number of photons emitted in one minute.
questions.answer: About 2.1 x 10^19 photons in one minute (1.9 x 10^19 if 0.10 W is used)
steps: The LED is 100% efficient, so light energy in one minute = 0.110 W x 60 s = 6.6 J.
Number of photons N = 6.6 / 3.17 x 10^-19 = 2.1 x 10^19.
Using the rounded power of 0.10 W instead gives 1.9 x 10^19.

questions.question: Red LED replaced with green LED (shorter wavelength) with same current. Explain effect on number of photons emitted per minute.
questions.answer: The number of photons per minute falls: each green photon has more energy, so the same power gives fewer photons.
steps: Same current and (approximately) same p.d. means the same power output.
Photon energy E = hc / lambda is higher for shorter wavelength.
Number of photons per second = P / E is lower, so fewer photons are emitted per minute.

questions.topic: Intensity from LED Compared to Sunlight
questions.question: LED power 0.69 W; at 5.0 mm the intensity is claimed greater than sunlight intensity 1100 W m^-2. Assess this.
questions.answer: Correct: intensity is about 2.2 x 10^3 W m^-2, which is greater than 1100 W m^-2 (assuming the LED radiates equally in all directions).
steps: Intensity I = P / (4 pi r^2), assuming isotropic emission.
This is greater than 1100 W m^-2, so the student's suggestion is correct.

questions.question: Explain how current and p.d. measurements could show charge and energy are conserved in a circuit with identical resistors A, B and C.
questions.answer: Show that I_C = I_A + I_B (charge) and E = V_C + V_A (energy), using ammeters and voltmeters.
steps: Measure the current in C (I_C), in A (I_A) and in B (I_B) with ammeters placed in series with each resistor.
Charge is conserved, so the charge per second arriving at the junction equals the charge per second leaving: I_C = I_A + I_B. Because A and B are identical and in parallel, I_A = I_B = I_C / 2.
Measure the p.d. across the cell (E), across C (V_C) and across the parallel pair A and B (V_A = V_B) with voltmeters in parallel with each.
Energy is conserved, so the energy per unit charge supplied by the cell equals the energy per unit charge transferred in C and then in A (or B): E = V_C + V_A.
Equivalently, multiply by the current: the power supplied E I_C equals the total power dissipated V_C I_C + V_A I_A + V_B I_B.
Readings agree within the uncertainty of the meters, which shows that charge and energy are both conserved.

questions.question: Three identical 12.5 ohm resistors in the circuit shown. Calculate the total resistance.
questions.answer: Total resistance = 18.8 ohm
steps: A and B are in parallel: 1/R = 1/12.5 + 1/12.5 = 2/12.5, so R = 6.25 ohm.
C is in series with this parallel section: R_total = 12.5 + 6.25 = 18.75 ohm, which is 18.8 ohm.

questions.topic: Internal Resistance from Single Ammeter Reading
questions.question: Describe how a single ammeter reading can determine the internal resistance of the cell, showing where the ammeter goes on the diagram.
questions.answer: Put an ammeter in series with the cell (in the main line, e.g. next to C). Then r = E / I - 18.75 ohm.
steps: Add the ammeter in the main loop in series with the cell and resistor C, so it reads the total current I from the cell.
The total resistance of the circuit is the external resistance (18.75 ohm from part (b)(i)) plus the internal resistance r.
E = I (R_external + r), so r = E / I - 18.75 ohm, using the known e.m.f. E and the ammeter reading I.

questions.question: Cell e.m.f. 1.54 V with negligible internal resistance; ammeter reads 0.14 A. Calculate the resistance of R.
questions.answer: R = 6.0 ohm
steps: Total resistance: R_total = E / I = 1.54 / 0.14 = 11.0 ohm (negligible internal resistance).
The 9.0 ohm resistor is in series with the parallel pair (3.0 ohm and R), so the parallel section is 11.0 - 9.0 = 2.0 ohm.

questions.question: Thin copper wire diameter 0.15 mm. Show the cross-sectional area is about 2 x 10^-8 m^2.
Calculate the length of copper wire used to make the 9.0 ohm resistor, given copper resistivity 1.68 x 10^-8 ohm m.
steps: Rearrange R = rho L / A to give L = R A / rho.

questions.question: Copper wire: charge carrier density 8.49 x 10^28 m^-3, current 0.14 A. Calculate the drift velocity of the electrons.
steps: Use I = n A e v, so v = I / (n A e).

questions.topic: Electrons Passing a Point per Second
questions.question: Calculate the number of electrons passing point X each second in the circuit shown.
questions.answer: Number of electrons per second = 4.2 x 10^18
steps: The 3.0 ohm and 6.0 ohm resistors are in parallel: R = 3.0 x 6.0 / 9.0 = 2.0 ohm. Total R = 4.0 + 2.0 = 6.0 ohm.
Total current I = 12 / 6.0 = 2.0 A. P.d. across the parallel section = 2.0 x 2.0 = 4.0 V.
Current through the 6.0 ohm resistor (at X) = 4.0 / 6.0 = 0.667 A.
Electrons per second = I / e = 0.667 / 1.60 x 10^-19 = 4.2 x 10^18.

questions.topic: Effect of Added Resistor on Current
questions.question: Resistor Y is added to the circuit; evaluate the student's statement.
questions.answer: The first two parts are correct, but the conclusion is wrong: the total power decreases.
steps: Y is in series with the 3.0 ohm resistor, so that branch has more resistance and the resistance of the parallel section increases. The first statement is correct.
This makes the total resistance of the circuit increase, which is also correct.
However, the current from the battery then decreases. P = I^2 R cannot be used to compare because I does not stay the same.

With a fixed e.m.f. of 12 V (negligible internal resistance), P = E^2 / R_total, so a larger R_total gives a smaller power. The total power decreases, so the student is wrong about the overall effect.

questions.question: NTC thermistor and fixed resistor in circuit; thermistor temperature increases. Which table row shows the changes to ammeter and voltmeter readings?
questions.answer: D: ammeter reading increases; voltmeter reading increases
steps: Raising the temperature of an NTC thermistor lowers its resistance, so the total resistance of the circuit falls and the current (ammeter) increases.
The voltmeter is across the fixed resistor, so V = I R increases because I increases, which is row D.

questions.question: Ammeter reads 23 mA in a thermistor circuit with a negligible-resistance supply. Show that the voltmeter reading was about 6 V.
steps: The 500 ohm and 600 ohm resistors are in parallel: R = 500 x 600 / (500 + 600) = 273 ohm.
The ammeter current (23 mA) passes through this parallel pair, so the voltmeter across it reads V = I R = 0.023 x 273.
V = 6.3 V, which is about 6 V.

questions.question: Calculate the power dissipated by the thermistor, using the voltmeter reading of about 6 V and ammeter reading 23 mA.
steps: Power P = V I (p.d. across the thermistor multiplied by current through it).

questions.question: The student decreases the temperature of the thermistor. Explain the effect on the ammeter and voltmeter readings.
questions.answer: The ammeter reading decreases and the voltmeter reading decreases.
steps: Lowering the temperature of the NTC thermistor means fewer conduction electrons are released, so its resistance increases.
The total resistance of the circuit increases, so with a constant 12 V the current falls and the ammeter reading decreases.
The voltmeter is across the fixed parallel pair (273 ohm), so V = I R decreases because I decreases.
The p.d. across the thermistor rises, because the sum of the p.d.s remains 12 V.

questions.question: Resistivity paper has length 12.0 cm and width 4.2 cm between ends; resistance 8.8 ohm; carbon resistivity 3.7 x 10^-5 ohm m. Calculate the thickness of the carbon layer.
steps: Resistance R = rho L / A, where the cross-sectional area A = width x thickness.
Rearrange: t = rho L / (R x w).

questions.question: Cell of e.m.f. 1.5 V connected across resistivity paper (resistance 8.8 ohm); voltmeter reads 1.4 V. Calculate the internal resistance of the cell.
questions.answer: r = 0.63 ohm
steps: Lost volts in cell = E - V = 1.5 - 1.4 = 0.1 V.
r = lost volts / I = 0.1 / 0.159 = 0.63 ohm.

questions.question: The right-hand voltmeter connection is moved to 3.0 cm from the left-hand end of the 12.0 cm paper. Determine the voltmeter reading.
steps: The paper is uniform, so p.d. is proportional to length along it.
The p.d. across 12.0 cm is 1.4 V, so p.d. across 3.0 cm = 1.4 x 3.0 / 12.0 = 0.35 V.

questions.question: In 60 s, 4.80 x 10^20 electrons pass point Z. Show the current at Z is about 1.3 A.
questions.answer: I = 1.28 A, about 1.3 A.
steps: Total charge Q = n e = 4.80 x 10^20 x 1.60 x 10^-19 = 76.8 C.
Current I = Q / t = 76.8 / 60 = 1.28 A, about 1.3 A.

questions.question: In 60 s the resistor transfers 24 J of energy. Calculate the potential difference across the resistor.
steps: Same charge passes the resistor: Q = 76.8 C from part (a).
Energy transferred E = V Q, so V = E / Q = 24 / 76.8 = 0.31 V.

questions.question: Intensity of light incident on an LDR decreases. Which row of the table is correct?
questions.answer: A: ammeter reading decreases; voltmeter reading decreases
steps: Less light on an LDR means fewer conduction electrons, so its resistance increases.
The total resistance of the circuit increases, so the current (ammeter) decreases.
The voltmeter is across the fixed resistor, V = I R, and so the reading decreases. This is row A.

questions.question: A temperature sensing circuit switches on a heater when the p.d. across the thermistor exceeds 0.7 V. Using the resistance-temperature graph, deduce whether the heater switches on when temperature falls below 10 C.
questions.answer: Yes: at 10 degrees C the p.d. across the thermistor is 0.71 V, which is above 0.7 V, so the heater switches on.
steps: From the graph, the thermistor resistance at 10 degrees C is about 2.0 ohm.
The 15 ohm resistor and the thermistor are a potential divider across 6.0 V: V_thermistor = 6.0 x 2.0 / (15 + 2.0).
V = 0.71 V, which is greater than 0.7 V.
Below 10 degrees C the thermistor resistance rises further, so its p.d. is even larger and the heater switches on.

questions.question: Explain why the resistance of the thermistor changes with temperature.
questions.answer: As temperature rises more electrons are released into the conduction band, so there are more charge carriers and resistance falls (NTC).
steps: A thermistor is a semiconductor with few free charge carriers at low temperature.
As temperature increases, thermal energy frees more electrons into the conduction band.
More charge carriers means lower resistance (negative temperature coefficient).

questions.topic: Minimum PD for Headlight to Emit Light
questions.question: A headlight emits light when it dissipates at least 35 W. Using its I-V graph, determine the minimum p.d. for light emission.
questions.answer: Minimum p.d. = 9.0 V
steps: The headlight emits light when P = V I >= 35 W, so read pairs (V, I) from the graph and calculate V I.
At 7.5 V, I = 3.57 A, so P = 26.8 W (too low). At 9.0 V, I = 3.93 A, so P = 35.4 W (just enough).
At 10.5 V, I = 4.27 A, P = 44.8 W, so the 35 W point is at the 9.0 V value.
Minimum p.d. is about 9.0 V.

questions.question: Explain the advantages of connecting two headlights in parallel with the battery rather than in series.
questions.answer: In parallel each lamp gets the full 12 V and works normally, and one lamp failing does not switch off the other.
steps: In parallel each headlight has the full 12.0 V across it, so each can operate at its rated power.
In series the p.d. would be shared, so each lamp would be too dim.
Parallel branches are independent: if one headlight fails (open circuit) the other stays on.
Each headlight can be switched on and off independently.

questions.question: Two headlights are connected to a 12.0 V battery. A student says the parallel combined resistance is one quarter of the series combined resistance. Deduce whether this is correct, using the graph.
questions.answer: Not correct: the ratio is about 0.35, not 0.25.
steps: Parallel: each headlight has 12.0 V across it, so from the graph I = 4.6 A each. Total I = 9.2 A, so R_parallel = 12 / 9.2 = 1.3 ohm.
Series: the identical headlights share the 12.0 V, so each has 6.0 V. From the graph, I = 3.2 A, so R_series = 12 / 3.2 = 3.8 ohm.
Ratio R_parallel / R_series = 1.3 / 3.8 = 0.35, not one quarter.
The quarter rule only holds for a fixed resistance. A filament lamp has a resistance that rises with p.d. (heating), so the student is incorrect.

questions.question: Current 4.60 A in copper wire; n = 8.49 x 10^28 m^-3; resistivity 1.72 x 10^-8 ohm m; resistance per unit length 1.75 x 10^-2 ohm m^-1. Calculate the drift velocity of electrons.
steps: Cross-sectional area A = rho / (resistance per unit length) = 1.72 x 10^-8 / 1.75 x 10^-2 = 9.83 x 10^-7 m^2.
Current I = n A e v, so v = I / (n A e).

questions.question: Two resistors are connected in a circuit with an expression given for their combined resistance. Derive this expression.
steps: The resistors are in parallel, so the p.d. across each is the supply p.d. V.
Charge is conserved at the junction, so I = I1 + I2, with I1 = V / R1 and I2 = V / R2.
The combined resistance is R = V / I = V / (V / R1 + V / R2) = 1 / (1/R1 + 1/R2).
Combine over a common denominator: 1/R1 + 1/R2 = (R1 + R2) / (R1 R2), so R = R1 R2 / (R1 + R2).

questions.topic: EMF and Internal Resistance from Graph
questions.question: Determine the e.m.f. and internal resistance of the cell from the student's V against I graph.
questions.answer: E.m.f. = 1.50 V; internal resistance = 0.75 ohm
steps: The voltmeter is across the cell, so V = E - I r: the y-intercept is the e.m.f. and the gradient is -r.
Extrapolate the line back to I = 0: V = 1.50 V, so E = 1.50 V.
So r = 0.75 ohm.

questions.question: An identical cell is placed in series with the original cell. Describe how the new V-I graph differs from the graph for one cell.
questions.answer: The y-intercept (e.m.f.) doubles and the gradient (internal resistance) doubles, so the line is steeper and starts higher.
steps: Two identical cells in series give total e.m.f. 2E.
Total internal resistance is 2r.
So the V-I line has intercept 2E and gradient magnitude 2r: higher intercept and steeper slope.

questions.topic: Derive Cell Equation for Resistance Graph
questions.question: Show that, for the circuit with variable resistor R and cell of e.m.f. E and internal resistance r, the required linear relation holds (the equation is shown in the figure below).
questions.answer: R = E / I - r
steps: The e.m.f. equals the sum of the p.d.s around the circuit: E = I R + I r.
Divide by I: E / I = R + r.
Rearranging gives R = E / I - r.

questions.topic: EMF and Internal Resistance from Graph
questions.question: From the graph of R against the plotted quantity, determine the e.m.f. and internal resistance of the cell.
questions.answer: E.m.f. = 1.5 V; internal resistance = 2.0 ohm
steps: R = E (1/I) - r compares with y = m x + c: the gradient is the e.m.f. and the y-intercept is -r.
Gradient = (10 - 2) / (8.0 - 2.7) = 1.5 V (reading the points (2.7, 2) and (8.0, 10)). So E = 1.5 V.
The line cuts the R axis at -2.0 ohm, so r = 2.0 ohm.

questions.topic: Power in Internal Resistance vs R
questions.question: A student suggests the power dissipated by the internal resistance r decreases as R increases. Comment on this suggestion, without further calculation.
questions.answer: Correct: as R increases the current falls, and power in the internal resistance P = I^2 r falls as the square of the current.
steps: As R increases, total resistance R + r increases, so I = E/(R + r) decreases.
Power in the internal resistance P = I^2 r.
Since r is constant and I decreases, P decreases.
So the student's suggestion is correct.

questions.question: A second identical cell is added in series with the first and the experiment repeated. Add a line to the graph to show the result.
questions.answer: Draw a steeper straight line: R = 3.0 / I - 4.0, with y-intercept -4.0 ohm and the same x-intercept 1.33 A^-1.
steps: Two identical cells in series: E doubles (3.0 V) and r doubles (4.0 ohm).
The new relationship is R = (3.0 / I) - 4.0, so the gradient becomes 3.0 (twice the original 1.5) and the intercept on the R axis is -4.0 ohm.
The line still crosses the 1/I axis at 4.0 / 3.0 = 1.33 A^-1, the same point as the original line.
It also passes through (4.0, 8.0) and (6.0, 14), so it lies above the original line at larger 1/I.

questions.question: Explain why the power dissipated by the whole circuit changes as light intensity on the LDR increases, referring to the LDR resistance.
questions.answer: More light lowers the LDR resistance, so the total resistance falls, the current rises, and the total power P = EI increases.
steps: Greater light intensity releases more electrons into the conduction band in the LDR.
So the LDR resistance decreases.
Total resistance of the series circuit falls, so the current I = E / R_total increases.
Total power dissipated P = E I (e.m.f. is constant) increases.

questions.question: The current in a uniform wire is constant. Which graph shows how p.d. across the wire varies with its length? (Options are graphs.)
questions.answer: C
steps: For a uniform wire with constant current, V = I R and R = rho L / A, so V = (I rho / A) L.
V is directly proportional to length: a straight line through the origin, which is graph C.

questions.question: Explain how the counterweight affects the work required from the motor to raise the lift.
questions.answer: The counterweight balances part of the lift's weight, so the motor does less work to raise the lift.
steps: The counterweight's weight acts in the opposite direction to the lift's weight.
So the net load the motor must lift is smaller.
Work done by the motor = (lift weight - counterweight weight) x height is therefore reduced.

questions.question: The motor raises the lift 40.0 m in 30.0 s. Lift and people 2250 kg, counterweight 1300 kg. Show that the output power is about 12 kW.
questions.answer: P = 12.4 kW, about 12 kW.
steps: Net mass moved by motor = 2250 - 1300 = 950 kg.
Work done W = m g h = 950 x 9.81 x 40.0 = 3.73 x 10^5 J.

questions.question: The motor dissipates energy to the surroundings at 3600 W. Determine the efficiency of the motor.
questions.answer: Efficiency = 0.78 (78%)
steps: Input power = useful output power + wasted power = 12.4 kW + 3.6 kW = 16.0 kW.
Efficiency = output / input = 12.4 / 16.0 = 0.78, or 78%.

questions.question: A student connects four resistors between points X and Y. Which expression gives the total resistance between X and Y?
steps: The 7 ohm and 18 ohm resistors are in parallel: 1 / (1/7 + 1/18).
The 4 ohm resistor is connected in parallel with a plain wire (short circuit), so no current flows through it and it contributes nothing to the resistance.
The 15 ohm resistor is in series with the parallel pair, so R = 15 + 1 / (1/7 + 1/18), option C.

questions.question: A circuit includes a thermistor; the temperature increases. Which row of the table shows how the ammeter and voltmeter readings change?
questions.answer: D: ammeter reading increases; voltmeter reading increases
steps: Raising the temperature of the thermistor lowers its resistance, so the total resistance falls and the current (ammeter reading) increases.
The voltmeter is across the fixed resistor, V = I R, so it increases as well, which is row D.

questions.question: A high resistance voltmeter is connected across a battery with no other components. Explain why its reading gives the e.m.f.
questions.answer: A high resistance voltmeter draws almost no current, so there is no lost volts across the internal resistance and the reading equals the e.m.f.
steps: Voltmeter resistance is very high, so the current through the battery is almost zero.
With no current, there is no p.d. (Ir) lost inside the battery.
So the terminal p.d. equals the e.m.f.

questions.question: Draw a circuit diagram to investigate how p.d. V across a battery varies with current I.
questions.answer: Battery in series with an ammeter and a variable resistor; a voltmeter connected across the battery terminals.
steps: Draw a series loop of the battery, an ammeter and a variable resistor (the variable resistor changes the current I).
Connect a voltmeter in parallel across the battery terminals, to read the p.d. V across the battery.
Use the correct symbols (ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel, variable resistor with an arrow).

questions.topic: EMF and Internal Resistance from Graph
questions.question: From the student's graph of V against I, determine the e.m.f. and internal resistance of the battery.
questions.answer: E.m.f. = 8.8 V; internal resistance = 2.3 ohm
steps: V = E - I r: the y-intercept of the line is the e.m.f. and the gradient is -r.
The best-fit line meets the V axis at 8.8 V, so E = 8.8 V.
Check: the line meets the I axis at I = 8.8 / 2.3 = 3.8 A, in agreement with the graph.

questions.question: Explain why there is a maximum current that can be supplied by the battery.
questions.answer: The maximum current occurs when the external resistance is zero (short circuit): I = E / r, limited only by the internal resistance.
steps: Current I = E / (R + r).
As the external resistance R falls towards zero, the current rises.
It cannot exceed E / r because the internal resistance r always limits it.

questions.question: Copper wires connect nichrome wire to a cell; wires have the same diameter; copper has more conduction electrons per m^3. Compare the average electron velocity in the copper and nichrome.
questions.answer: The electrons in the copper wires have a lower average (drift) velocity than in the nichrome wire, since the current is the same and copper has a higher carrier density.
steps: The copper and nichrome are in series, so the current I is the same in both.
Drift velocity v = I / (n A e), with the same area A for both wires (same diameter).
Copper has a greater n, so v is smaller in copper.
Hence the electrons in the copper move more slowly than in the nichrome.

questions.question: State what is meant by the resistivity of a material.
questions.answer: Resistivity is the resistance of a sample of unit length and unit cross-sectional area of the material (rho = R A / L).
steps: Resistivity is a property of the material, independent of its size.
It is the resistance of a 1 m length with a 1 m^2 cross-sectional area, rho = RA / L.

questions.question: Describe how the student could determine the resistivity of the conducting material from a sample.
questions.answer: Measure resistance R by V/I, measure length L and cross-sectional area A, then rho = RA/L; repeat and average.
steps: Measure the length L of the sample with a ruler and its width and thickness (or diameter) to find A.
Connect the sample to a cell, ammeter and voltmeter and measure V and I to find R = V / I.
Calculate resistivity rho = R A / L.
Repeat for several readings and average to reduce random error.

questions.topic: Copper Low Resistivity and Drift Velocity
questions.question: Explain how the low resistivity of copper affects the drift velocity of electrons in the copper electrodes.
questions.answer: Copper has a high density of conduction electrons, so for the same current the drift velocity of electrons in the copper is low.
steps: Low resistivity means copper has a very high number density of charge carriers n.
Drift velocity v = I / (n A e), so for a given current v is small when n is large.
So electrons in the copper electrodes drift slowly, and the electrodes carry current with little heating.

questions.question: Explain how adding panels in parallel changes the power output of the heating system.
questions.answer: Adding panels in parallel lowers the total resistance, so more current is drawn and the power output increases.
steps: Panels in parallel: total resistance falls as more branches are added.
For a fixed supply p.d. V, the power output P = V^2 / R_total increases.
So the power output increases.

questions.question: A system uses five heating panels with resistivity 6.4 x 10^-3 ohm m and thickness 0.48 mm. Maximum power must be below 350 W. Deduce whether the design is safe.
questions.answer: Not safe: the maximum power is about 680 W, which is more than 350 W.
steps: Current flows across the panel between the electrodes, so L = 0.51 m and A = width x thickness = 1.60 m x 0.48 x 10^-3 m = 7.68 x 10^-4 m^2.
Resistance of one panel R = rho L / A = 6.4 x 10^-3 x 0.51 / 7.68 x 10^-4 = 4.25 ohm.
The panels are connected in parallel across 24 V, so P of one panel = V^2 / R = 24^2 / 4.25 = 136 W.
Five panels: total P = 5 x 136 = 680 W (equivalently V^2 / (R / 5)), which is greater than 350 W, so the design is not safe.

questions.topic: Derive EMF Equation for Thermistor Circuit
questions.question: A thermistor is in series with a wire resistor of resistance R. At 45 C the thermistor resistance is four times R, and the power P dissipated in the resistor is 0.38 W. Derive the equation P = V^2 / R.
questions.answer: P = I V and I = V / R, so P = V x V / R = V^2 / R.
steps: Power is the rate of energy transfer: P = I V.
From the definition of resistance, V = I R, so I = V / R.
Substitute for I: P = (V / R) x V = V^2 / R.

questions.topic: Battery Potential Difference from Thermistor Circuit
questions.question: Determine the potential difference across the battery given P = 0.38 W at 45 C.
questions.answer: P.d. across the battery = 9.1 V
steps: Read the thermistor resistance at 45 degrees C from the graph: about 35 ohm. So the resistor has R = 35 / 4 = 8.75 ohm.
P.d. across the resistor: P = V^2 / R, so V = sqrt(P R) = sqrt(0.38 x 8.75) = 1.82 V.
The resistor has one fifth of the total resistance (R + 4R = 5R) in the series circuit, so the battery p.d. is 5 x 1.82 V.

questions.question: Explain why the resistance of a thermistor decreases as temperature increases.
questions.answer: Higher temperature frees more electrons from the lattice into the conduction band, so there are more charge carriers and resistance falls.
steps: A thermistor is a semiconductor with few free electrons at low temperature.
Increasing temperature gives electrons enough thermal energy to move into the conduction band.
More charge carriers means lower resistance.

questions.question: Both the wire resistor and thermistor are heated from 80 C to 90 C. Explain why the current in the circuit decreases.
questions.answer: The resistance of the wire rises by more than the thermistor resistance falls, so the total resistance increases and the current decreases.
steps: When the temperature rises, the thermistor resistance decreases because more electrons are released as conduction electrons. However, between 80 and 90 degrees C the graph is nearly flat, so the decrease is small.
The metal wire has a roughly constant number of conduction electrons but its lattice ions vibrate with larger amplitude.
The conduction electrons collide with the ions more frequently, so the resistance of the wire increases.
The total resistance of the series circuit is the sum of both resistances, so it increases because the wire resistance rises more than the thermistor resistance falls.
With a fixed battery e.m.f., I = E / R_total, so the current in the circuit decreases.

questions.question: A cell is connected to two resistors. Which expression gives the power transferred by the 20 ohm resistor?
steps: The resistors are in series, so the current is I = 1.5 / (20 + 30).
The p.d. across the 20 ohm resistor is V = 1.5 x 20 / (20 + 30) (potential divider).
Power P = V I = [1.5 x 20 / (20 + 30)] x [1.5 / (20 + 30)], which is option C.

questions.question: Describe the photoelectric effect.
questions.answer: Electrons are emitted from a metal surface when electromagnetic radiation of sufficiently high frequency is incident on it.
steps: Electromagnetic radiation incident on a metal surface transfers energy to electrons, one photon per electron.
If the photon frequency is above the threshold frequency, electrons are emitted immediately.
Emission depends on frequency, not on intensity.

questions.question: Explain why the photomultiplier cannot detect some frequencies of electromagnetic radiation.
questions.answer: Photons below the threshold frequency have energy hf less than the work function, so they cannot release electrons.
steps: Photon energy E = hf.
If hf is less than the work function of the photocathode, no electron is emitted.
So low-frequency radiation is not detected.

questions.question: Visible light spans 380 nm to 700 nm; the photocathode work function is 1.48 eV. Deduce whether the photomultiplier detects all visible wavelengths.
questions.answer: Yes: the threshold wavelength is about 840 nm, which is longer than 700 nm, so all visible light releases electrons.
steps: Threshold wavelength: lambda = hc / phi = 1240 eV nm / 1.48 eV = 838 nm.
Light is detected only if its wavelength is shorter than the threshold, i.e. below about 838 nm.
The longest visible wavelength is 700 nm, which is less than 838 nm, so all visible wavelengths are detected.

questions.question: An electron leaves the photocathode at 1.35 x 10^6 m s^-1, with p.d. 108 V to the first plate. Calculate its kinetic energy when it hits the plate.
questions.answer: Kinetic energy = 1.81 x 10^-17 J
steps: Work done by the field = e V = 1.60 x 10^-19 x 108 = 1.73 x 10^-17 J.

questions.question: Four 85.0 k ohm resistors A to D apply p.d. between plates. With switch open the supply p.d. is 1960 V; with switch closed the p.d. across A is 108 V. Calculate the internal resistance of the supply.
questions.answer: Internal resistance = 1.2 x 10^6 ohm
steps: Open switch: no current, so the e.m.f. of the supply is 1960 V.
Switch closed: the four 85.0 k ohm resistors are in series, so I = 108 / 85 000 = 1.27 x 10^-3 A, and the p.d. across the chain is 4 x 108 = 432 V.
Lost volts = 1960 - 432 = 1528 V.

questions.question: Circuit with a cell of internal resistance 0.5 ohm. Which expression gives the e.m.f. of the cell?
steps: The voltmeter reads the p.d. across the 6 ohm resistor (1.2 V), so I = 1.2 / 6.
Lost volts across the internal resistance = I r = (1.2 / 6) x 0.5.

questions.question: The diagram shows part of a circuit. Which expression gives the total resistance between X and Y?
steps: The 2 ohm and 3 ohm resistors are in series: (2 + 3).
This is in parallel with the 4 ohm resistor: 1 / [1/(2 + 3) + 1/4].
The 6 ohm resistor is in series with the parallel section, so add 6, which is option D (total 8.2 ohm).

questions.question: Battery with negligible internal resistance; R1 and R2 identical. Which expression gives the p.d. across R1?
steps: The battery e.m.f. is 10 V (negligible internal resistance), and the voltmeter shows 3.3 V across the first resistor.
The p.d. across the parallel pair (R1 and R2) is 10 - 3.3 = 6.7 V.
In a parallel section each branch has the same p.d. as the section, so the p.d. across R1 is 10 - 3.3 (the 1/2 in option C would be wrong).

questions.question: A student connects a circuit with resistors of different resistances. Which expression gives the current in resistor R?
steps: The voltmeter reads 1.4 V across the 4.7 ohm resistor, which is in the main branch with the cell, so it carries the total current: I = 1.4 / 4.7.
This current splits between resistor R and the lower branch with the ammeter (0.13 A).
Charge conservation: I_R = 1.4 / 4.7 - 0.13, option A.

questions.question: A 1.5 V cell with negligible internal resistance is in a circuit with two resistors and a voltmeter; the switch is closed. What is the reading? A 0.15 V, B 0.50 V, C 1.00 V, D 1.50 V.
steps: The closed switch is in parallel with the 5 ohm resistor, so it short-circuits it and no current flows through the 5 ohm resistor.
The circuit then has the 10 ohm resistor only, directly across the 1.5 V cell (negligible internal resistance).
The voltmeter across the 10 ohm resistor reads 1.50 V.

questions.question: A uniform wire on a metre rule carries current; the distance d between voltmeter connections is increased. Which graph shows V against d?
questions.answer: C
steps: The current in the uniform wire is constant and R = rho L / A, so the p.d. between the connections is V = I rho d / A.
V is directly proportional to d, so the graph is a straight line through the origin, graph C.

questions.topic: Security Lamp LDR Fixed Resistor PD
questions.question: Light intensity on the LDR decreases in a security lamp circuit. Explain what happens to the p.d. across the fixed resistor.
questions.answer: The p.d. across the fixed resistor decreases, because the LDR resistance rises, the current falls and V = IR for the fixed resistor falls.
steps: Lower light intensity means the LDR resistance increases.
Total resistance increases, so the current falls.
p.d. across the fixed resistor = I R falls, since R is constant.

questions.question: The lamp switches on when the p.d. across the fixed resistor is 0.62 V. The ratio of LDR resistance to fixed resistance is 3:2 and the current is 28 mA. Calculate the LDR resistance.
questions.answer: Resistance of LDR = 33 ohm (about 33.2 ohm)
steps: Fixed resistor R_f = V / I = 0.62 / 0.028 = 22.1 ohm.
Ratio LDR : fixed = 3 : 2, so R_LDR = (3/2) x 22.1 = 33.2 ohm.
Resistance of LDR = 33 ohm.

questions.question: Explain why the ray of light refracts at surface X of the glass prism.
questions.answer: Light changes speed when it enters glass from air, so it changes direction (refracts) at the surface.
steps: Light travels slower in glass (higher refractive index) than in air.
When the ray enters the glass at an angle, the change in speed causes a change in direction at surface X.

questions.topic: Total Internal Reflection at Prism Face
questions.question: Deduce whether a silver layer is needed on surface Y of the prism with refractive index 1.52.
questions.answer: Yes, a silver layer is needed: the angle of incidence at Y (37 degrees) is less than the critical angle (41 degrees).
steps: The 53 degrees shown is the angle between the ray and the surface, so the angle of incidence (to the normal) is 90 - 53 = 37 degrees.
Critical angle: sin C = 1 / n = 1 / 1.52, so C = 41 degrees.
Total internal reflection needs the angle of incidence to be greater than C. Since 37 degrees < 41 degrees, there is no total internal reflection, so the ray is partly transmitted.
A silver layer is therefore needed on Y to reflect the light.

questions.question: Explain why knowing the number of photons arriving per second on a sensor of known area cannot give the light intensity.
questions.answer: Intensity is power per unit area, and each photon carries energy hc/lambda, which depends on wavelength, so a photon count alone does not give power.
steps: Intensity = power incident per unit area.
Power = (number of photons per second) x (energy per photon).
Energy per photon depends on wavelength (E = hc/lambda), which is not given, so the photon count alone is not enough.

questions.question: Monochromatic light at 600 nm with power 1.0 W is incident on the sensor. Determine the percentage of photons detected by the sensor.
questions.answer: About 85 % of the photons are detected
steps: From the graph, the current at 600 nm is about 0.41 A.
Number of electrons per second (one per detected photon) = I / e = 0.41 / 1.60 x 10^-19 = 2.6 x 10^18 s^-1.
Photon energy E = h c / lambda = 6.63 x 10^-34 x 3.00 x 10^8 / 600 x 10^-9 = 3.3 x 10^-19 J, so photons arriving per second = 1.0 / 3.3 x 10^-19 = 3.0 x 10^18 s^-1.
Percentage detected = 2.6 x 10^18 / 3.0 x 10^18 x 100 = 85 %.

questions.question: Draw a circuit diagram the student could use to investigate the LED's current against p.d.
questions.answer: LED in series with a cell, a variable resistor and an ammeter; voltmeter across the LED; LED connected the right way round (forward biased).
steps: Draw a series circuit: power supply (cell), variable resistor (or a potential divider), ammeter and the LED, with the LED symbol pointing in the direction of conventional current.
The ammeter is in series with the LED to measure its current.
The voltmeter is connected in parallel across the LED only, to measure the p.d. across it.

questions.question: Determine the power of the LED when the p.d. across it is 2.2 V, using the graph.
questions.answer: Power = 8.4 x 10^-2 W
steps: Read the current from the graph at 2.2 V: I = 38 mA = 0.038 A.
Power P = V I = 2.2 x 0.038.

questions.question: Describe, without calculation, how the resistance of the LED changes as the p.d. increases from 0 V to 2.4 V.
questions.answer: Resistance is very large at first (almost no current below about 1.6 V), then decreases rapidly above this threshold, and then decreases more slowly.
steps: From 0 to about 1.6 V the current is almost zero, so V / I is very large (the LED does not conduct).
Above 1.6 V the current increases rapidly with p.d., so the resistance V / I decreases sharply.
By 2.4 V the graph is nearly a straight line with a constant steep gradient, and the resistance has fallen to about 46 ohm (2.4 V / 52 mA).

questions.question: Steel cable of diameter 12 mm has total resistance 0.078 ohm; resistivity of steel is 1.4 x 10^-7 ohm m. Calculate the length of the cable.
questions.answer: L = 63 m
steps: Cross-sectional area A = pi (d/2)^2 = pi (6.0 x 10^-3)^2 = 1.13 x 10^-4 m^2.
Resistance R = rho L / A, so L = R A / rho.

questions.question: Lightning gives a p.d. of 1.5 x 10^8 V between rod and ground, causing a current of 1.2 x 10^4 A for 70 s. Calculate the work done.

questions.topic: Drift Velocity in Copper Versus Steel Cable
questions.question: Copper cable replaces steel with same length and diameter and same p.d.; copper has lower resistivity and more conduction electrons per volume. A student says drift velocities are the same. Assess the statement.
questions.answer: The statement is not justified: copper has a lower resistivity (more current) but also a larger n (smaller drift velocity per unit current), so v is the same only by coincidence.
steps: For the same length and diameter, R = rho L / A is smaller for copper because its resistivity is lower, so I = V / R is larger with the same p.d.
Drift velocity v = I / (n A e): the larger current increases v, but the greater number of conduction electrons per unit volume n decreases v.
Combined: v = V / (rho L n e), so v is inversely proportional to rho x n. The speeds are equal only if the product rho n is the same for both materials, which is unlikely.

For example, copper resistivity is about 8 times less than steel (1.72 x 10^-8 against 1.4 x 10^-7 ohm m), so the current is much bigger and v is probably higher in copper. The statement is therefore not correct in general.

questions.question: The work function of layer 1 of a solar cell is 1.86 eV. Calculate the minimum frequency of light to release an electron.
steps: Work function in joules: phi = 1.86 x 1.60 x 10^-19 = 2.98 x 10^-19 J.
Minimum frequency f = phi / h = 2.98 x 10^-19 / 6.63 x 10^-34.

questions.topic: Removing Layer Effect on Electron Release Rate
questions.question: Layer 1 (greater work function than layer 2) is removed so all photons reach layer 2. Explain how this affects the rate at which electrons are released, assuming each layer absorbs all photons above its threshold frequency.
questions.answer: The rate of electron release is unchanged: all photons above layer 2's threshold are absorbed in either case, so the same number of electrons is released per second, just now only from layer 2.
steps: With layer 1 present, photons above f1 are absorbed by layer 1; photons between f2 and f1 pass on and are absorbed by layer 2.
Without layer 1, all photons above f2 reach and are absorbed by layer 2.
Intensity is constant, so the number of photons absorbed per second (and so electrons released per second) is the same.
Only the location of emission changes; the rate is unchanged.

questions.question: Two solar cells each with e.m.f. 5.0 V and internal resistance 0.80 ohm drive a 4.0 ohm resistor. Series gives 13 W. Deduce whether parallel connection gives less than half this power.
questions.answer: Correct: parallel gives about 5.2 W, which is less than half of 13 W (6.5 W).
steps: Series: E = 10.0 V, r = 1.60 ohm; I = 10.0 / (4.0 + 1.60) = 1.79 A; P = I^2 R = 12.8 W, consistent with 13 W.
Half of 13 W is 6.5 W; 5.2 W is less than 6.5 W, so the suggestion is correct.

questions.question: Explain how the resistance of the heated metal wire changes as its temperature increases.
questions.answer: The resistance increases: the metal ions vibrate more with greater amplitude, causing more frequent collisions with electrons.
steps: Temperature rises, so the metal ions in the lattice gain kinetic energy.
They vibrate with greater amplitude.
Electrons collide with the ions more often, reducing their drift, so resistance increases.

questions.question: Wire of resistance 0.67 ohm, diameter 0.51 mm and length 0.14 m. Calculate the resistivity at the cutting temperature.
questions.answer: rho = 9.8 x 10^-7 ohm m
steps: Cross-sectional area A = pi (d/2)^2 = pi (2.55 x 10^-4)^2 = 2.04 x 10^-7 m^2.
rho = 9.8 x 10^-7 ohm m.

questions.question: Voltmeter reads 3.6 V across the lamp; use the I-V graph to show the combined resistance of lamp and resistor is about 5 ohm.
questions.answer: Combined resistance = 3.6 V / 0.71 A = 5.1 ohm, about 5 ohm
steps: The voltmeter reads 3.6 V across the lamp-and-ammeter branch in parallel with the 15 ohm resistor, so the lamp also has 3.6 V across it.
From the graph, the lamp current at 3.6 V is about 0.47 A. The current in the 15 ohm resistor is 3.6 / 15 = 0.24 A.
Total current = 0.47 + 0.24 = 0.71 A.
Combined resistance = V / I = 3.6 / 0.71 = 5.1 ohm, which is about 5 ohm.

questions.topic: Power in Lamp and Resistor Circuit
questions.question: EMF 4.5 V, negligible internal resistance, and the lamp-plus-resistor combination has resistance about 5 ohm. Determine the power dissipated when the voltmeter reads 3.6 V.
steps: The variable resistor is in series with the lamp-and-resistor combination, so the battery current is the 0.71 A found in part (a).
The battery e.m.f. is 4.5 V and its internal resistance is negligible, so the power supplied to the whole circuit is P = E I.
(The variable resistor takes the remaining 4.5 - 3.6 = 0.9 V, so you cannot use I = 4.5 / 5.)

questions.question: Student connects a circuit; voltmeter reading is 6 V. Which expression gives the internal resistance of the battery?
steps: The voltmeter reads the terminal p.d. across the 10 ohm resistor: 6 V, so I = 6 / 10.
Lost volts = E - V = 9 - 6 = 3 V = I r.

questions.question: State what is meant by the e.m.f. of a cell.
questions.answer: The e.m.f. is the energy transferred per unit charge by the cell (from chemical to electrical energy) in driving charge round the whole circuit.
steps: E.m.f. is energy transferred per coulomb of charge passing through the cell.
This includes energy used within the cell (to overcome its internal resistance).

questions.topic: LDR Light Effect on Terminal PD
questions.question: The voltmeter measures the terminal p.d. of a cell in series with an LDR. Explain how increasing light intensity on the LDR affects the voltmeter reading.
questions.answer: Greater light lowers the LDR resistance, so the current rises; the lost volts Ir increase, so the terminal p.d. (voltmeter reading) decreases.
steps: Increasing light intensity releases more electrons into the conduction band in the LDR.
So the LDR resistance decreases.
Total resistance in the circuit falls, so the current I = E / (R + r) increases.
Lost volts Ir inside the cell increase.
Terminal p.d. V = E - Ir therefore decreases, so the voltmeter reading falls.

questions.question: A uniform copper wire of length L is measured with an ohmmeter; a length d of the wire has resistance R. Which gives the total resistance of the wire?
questions.answer: D: (L / d) x R
steps: For a uniform wire, resistance is directly proportional to length.
Length d has resistance R, so length L has resistance R x L / d, option D.

questions.question: Three identical resistors are connected in a circuit with an e.m.f. and negligible internal resistance. Which is equal to the voltmeter reading?
questions.answer: C: 2E / 3 (where E is the e.m.f.)
steps: The two identical resistors R in parallel give R / 2. This is in series with the third resistor R, so R_total = 1.5 R.
The voltmeter is across the single resistor R, so V = E x R / (1.5 R) = 2E / 3, option C.

questions.question: State what is meant by an e.m.f. of 6.00 V.
questions.answer: Each coulomb of charge passing through the battery gains 6.00 J of energy from the chemical store.
steps: An e.m.f. of 6.00 V means the battery transfers 6.00 J of energy per coulomb of charge that passes through it.

questions.question: Voltmeter reads 1.64 V; show the ammeter reads about 20 mA.
steps: The voltmeter reads 1.64 V across the parallel pair, so the p.d. across the 200 ohm resistor is 6.00 - 1.64 = 4.36 V.
The ammeter is in series with the 200 ohm resistor, so I = V / R = 4.36 / 200 = 0.0218 A.
This is 22 mA, which is about 20 mA.

questions.question: Determine the resistance of resistor X.
questions.answer: Resistance of X = 3.0 x 10^2 ohm
steps: Total current I = 21.8 mA (from part (i)). Current in the 100 ohm resistor = 1.64 / 100 = 16.4 mA.
Current in X = 21.8 - 16.4 = 5.4 mA (the current divides at the junction).
